opennyai_summary.final__facts:
The aforesaid case arose out of a private complaint filed by the 2nd respondent alleging the commission of offences under Sections 498A and 406 IPC.
The learned Magistrate took the complaint to files and issued summons to the accused.
The 1st accused is the husband of the 2nd respondent/complainant.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
Secondly, it is submitted that the complaint is hopelessly 2026:KER:19588 barred by limitation even as per the averments of the complainant in Annexure A1 complaint.
The present complaint has been filed on 23.04.2013, which is after a period of 3 years and 3 months from the above date when the complainant had left the matrimonial residence and ceased to have contacts with the accused.
7. As already pointed out by the learned Amicus Curiae, the complaint does not contain any specific allegations of cruelty as against the 2nd petitioner.
Apart from the omnibus statement that all the accused resorted to mental cruelty upon her by innuendos and other oral statements, there is nothing pointing to any specific overt act as against the 2nd petitioner.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
8. The decisions rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Kahkashan Kausar and Ors v. State of Bihar and Ors [(2022) 6 SCC 599] and Rajesh Chaddha v. State of Uttar Pradesh [AIR 2025 SC 2836] are relied on by the learned Amicus Curiae in support of the 2026:KER:19588 argument that the Apex Court has strongly deprecated the practice of roping in the in-laws by raising frivolous and fictitious allegations of matrimonial cruelty against them.
[(2007)13 SCC 165] in which it has been laid down that the question of limitation has to be looked into by the Trial Court and that the condonation of delay as envisaged under Section 473 Cr.P.C has to be resorted to only in such cases where the Trial Court is satisfied that the delay has been properly explained or it is necessary to do so in the interests of justice.
Therefore,
